text.p: Base metal markets largely traded in the plus column on Wednesday, with LME copper leading the way, although the pace of trading was slow and most markets closed off their highs.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau index fell 3.04 points to 241.85.

On the LME, copper's failure to break above $2,600 was well-signposted, with the market perhaps still overbought and some heavy resistance expected around $2,610 and above. Final three months business on the kerb was at $2,592 a tonne, up $10 from Tuesday's close.

Aluminium dutifully followed copper higher, but lacked real independent momentum and never looked like regaining levels above $1,600. Stocks continue to decline - down another 3,100 tonnes - but this is having little impact on prices. Last business was at $1,593, still up $9 with the market likely to range-trade between $1,570 and $1,600 in the short-term, traders said.
Nickel business was mostly low-key throughout, with little movement seen after an initial flip-up above $7,200, and the market closed at $7,230, a gain of $20.
Zinc flipped up to the highs of a tight day's trading range on the kerb in short-covering, building on the earlier trade buying. Last business was at $1,375, up $7 from Tuesday.
Lead continued to correct up from yesterday's 20-month lows, with some trade interest also seen, although the extent of the upmove was restricted. Prices closed with modest $2 gains at $624.
The tin market similarly steadied in tandem with the rest of the complex, but remains vulnerable to a re-test of recent one-year lows at $5,510. Last trade was at $5,580, up just $10.
Alloy was steadier when traded today, and closed at $1,472/75 a tonne, up from the previous close of $1,465.

CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed lower on commercial selling with a drop in soybeans also weighing on the market, traders said. There was increased talk about the El Nino weather phenomenon this year. The El Nino was leading to concerns about dry weather in Australia's wheat growing region. CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed unchanged to seven cents per bushel lower, with July down five at $3.38-3/4 and September closed seven lower at $3.45-1/4.

NYMEX oil prices ended sharply lower Wednesday with gasoline leading the decline as the torrid pace of refinery runs and record crude imports suggested a surfeit of petroleum. "Refiners are producing a record amount of gasoline when there is so much crude around. It seems refiners have enough of it (crude) as it is," said Sal Gugliara of United Energy. July crude finished 44 cents off at $18.79 a barrel while July gasoline settled a steep 1.70 cents off at 56.78 cents a gallon. July heating oil ended 1.01 cents a gallon lower at 51.44 cents.

COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended lower across the board Wednesday, with gold slipping to near four year lows on news of more European central bank gold sales, and platinum group metals lower as the date for the resumption of Russian exports draws nearer. "The Belgian plan to sell more gold via a bullion coin issue still needs parliamentary approval and will not impact until 1999, but the market just saw it as more evidence of a trend toward central bank gold sales and ended weaker," said Ted Kempf, an analyst with industry consultants CPM Group in New York. COMEX August gold ended down $2.80 at $341.00 an ounce, after seeing a new life-of-contract low at $340.60, with contract lows also being seen in the December 1997 and February 1998 delivery months. In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $338.90/40, not far from the four year low around $336.50 seen on February 15 this year.
